rows.notes: The study is a 'Case Report' that explicitly describes its method (Section 3) as an extensive literature review and analysis of secondary data (LIP borehole surveys, IWASRI salinity surveys, SMO observation wells, Figures 8-10 and Tables 1 and 4 all drawn from cited reports). It reports no experiment, survey or model run of its own; at most it compiles agency monitoring data. Even if treated as primary, it contains no evidence on drip or micro-irrigation: micro-irrigation is mentioned once (Section 6.1) as a recommended water-saving technique to accompany curtailment of surface supplies. What the study actually shows is that reduced canal supplies during the 1999-2002 drought coincided with lower water tables, reduced waterlogged area and no fall in crop yields in Sindh, and that waterlogging and surface salinity are driven by high surface irrigation allowances; this is about canal water allocation and conjunctive groundwater use, not about a shift from flood to micro-irrigation.

Same study characteristics as above: a review/case report built on secondary data with no own experiment or survey. It gives a groundwater balance for Sindh (Table 4, from Halcrow-ACE 2003) showing recharge from canal seepage and irrigation return flow and large non-beneficial evaporation losses, and argues that lowering canal supplies would reduce waterlogging. It does not examine micro-irrigation or drip at all, and does not report any result on drip reducing groundwater recharge; the only link is the general statement that recharge comes from canal seepage and irrigation return flows. Technology in the passage (micro-irrigation) is not the subject of the study.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is labelled a Case Report and is essentially a policy synthesis of secondary data on waterlogging, salinity and conjunctive use in the Lower Indus; it contains no drip or micro-irrigation evidence, so both claim rows receive all-'no' profiles regardless of whether Q1 is read as yes or no.
